concepts.title: Comparisons Made by Linear Search
concepts.definition: Linear search compares the key with each element from the first onwards and stops at the first match; the key sitting at zero-based index i costs i plus one comparisons, and the rest of the list stays unchecked.
concepts.key_idea: Finding 17 in [8, -4, 7, 17, 0, 2, 19] takes 4 comparisons because three elements precede it.
question_patterns: How many comparisons does linear search make to find 17 in the list [8, -4, 7, 17, 0, 2, 19]?
In the 15-element list of Activity 6.1, how many comparisons locate the key 12?
A key is found at index 4 of a 15-element list. How many elements were scanned and how many were left unchecked?
Why does linear search return the first match when a list holds duplicate values of the key?
Determine the position of 8, 1, 99 and 44 in the list [1, -2, 32, 8, 17, 19, 42, 13, 0, 44] by linear search and note the comparisons each takes.

solution_steps.explain: The match at zero-based index i ends a scan of i plus one elements.
Subtract the scan from the list size.

worked_examples.q: Finding 17 in [8, -4, 7, 17, 0, 2, 19] costs how many linear-search comparisons?

concepts.title: Best and Worst Work of Linear Search
concepts.definition: The workload of linear search swings with the key's location: a key at the front needs a single comparison, while a key at the last position, or one that is absent, forces comparisons with all n elements.
concepts.key_idea: Searching for 43 in an 11-element list that ends with 43 costs the full 11 comparisons.
question_patterns: Why does a key placed first cost only one comparison in linear search?
How many comparisons does linear search need when the key is the last element of an 11-element list?
How many comparisons does a failed linear search make on n elements?
In the list of Activity 6.2, how many comparisons find the key 43?
For which kind of lists is linear search still a sensible choice?

solution_steps.action: place the key in the list
solution_steps.explain: Front placement gives the best case of one comparison; last placement or absence gives the worst case of n comparisons.

worked_examples.q: What is the best-case comparison count for linear search?

concepts.title: Middle Position in Binary Search
concepts.definition: Binary search keeps two markers, first and last, on a sorted list and probes the midpoint computed by floor-dividing their sum by two, so for ten elements the probe lands on index 5, the sixth element.
concepts.key_idea: When the middle element equals the key the search ends immediately, as 17 found at index 7 shows.
question_patterns: Compute the mid index for first = 0 and last = 14 in a 15-element sorted list.
Why does floor division pick the sixth element as middle when a list holds ten elements?
A binary search runs from first = 0 to last = 6. Which index is probed next?
In the list of Example 6.2, why is key 17 found in a single iteration?
Which condition keeps the binary search loop running, and which comparison ends it?

solution_steps.explain: The span marker adds first and last.
Integer division by 2 rounds the midpoint down.

worked_examples.q: Binary search keeps first = 0 and last = 9 on a sorted list. Which midpoint index does (first + last) // 2 probe?

concepts.title: Halving the Search Area
concepts.definition: After every unsuccessful midpoint comparison, binary search discards half the remaining list, so a 15-element search area shrinks to 7, then 3, then 1 element across successive iterations.
concepts.key_idea: Searching key 2 in the 15-element list takes four iterations because 15 halves to 7, 3 and finally 1.
question_patterns: Starting with 15 elements, how many remain to be searched after three unsuccessful midpoint comparisons?
Why is the technique named binary search?
Searching key 2 in Example 6.2 takes how many iterations, and what sequence of search-area sizes passes by?
Which half is searched next when the middle element is greater than the key?
Does binary search rearrange the list during the search? Explain.

solution_steps.explain: After the first failed probe only one half stays in play.
The second iteration halves the survivors.
The third iteration leaves a single candidate.

worked_examples.q: A 15-element binary-search area halves after each unsuccessful comparison. How many elements remain after the first comparison?

concepts.title: Linear versus Binary Workload
concepts.definition: Locating a record at the exact middle of a sorted database costs one comparison for binary search but about half the database for linear search, which is why ordered data rewards binary searching enormously.
concepts.key_idea: For 2 to the power 30 records, a middle-position hit costs one comparison in binary search but 536870912 in linear search.
question_patterns: A sorted database holds 2 to the power 30 records and the wanted record sits in the middle. Estimate the comparisons each search needs.
Why is the term iteration preferred over comparison when describing binary search work?
What do you infer when a middle-of-file search costs 1 iteration for binary search but half a billion comparisons for linear search?
Which search would you choose for a sorted telephone directory and why?
Name two applications that build on binary search techniques.

solution_steps.explain: Two raised to the power 30 gives the record count.
A middle hit forces linear search through about half the records.

worked_examples.q: For 2^30 records, how many comparisons does a middle-position hit cost binary search?

concepts.title: Hash Value by Remainder Method
concepts.definition: Hashing computes an element's home slot directly: the remainder method divides the element by the hash table size and uses the remainder as the index, so checking presence needs just one comparison regardless of list size.
concepts.key_idea: In the table of size 10, element 16 lands in slot 6 and is reported at position 7.
question_patterns: Apply the hash function element % 10 to 16, 93 and 80 and give each one's slot.
Using h(element) = element % 11, where do 44, 121 and 55 land in the hash table?
Why does a hash-based search need only one key comparison?
Program 6-3 reports 16 at position 7. Show the arithmetic behind it.
Store the collection [44, 121, 55, 33, 110, 77, 22, 66] with h(element) = element % 11 and display the table.

solution_steps.explain: The remainder on division by the table size fixes the slot.
Program 6-3 adds one to print a human-friendly position.

worked_examples.q: Using the remainder method with a table of size 10, which zero-based slot does element 16 land in?

concepts.title: Collision and Perfect Hash Functions
concepts.definition: A collision happens when two elements share one hash slot, as 16 and 26 both mapping to 6 under a modulo-10 function; a hash function that gives every element a unique slot is called perfect, and collision resolution decides where the extras go.
concepts.key_idea: With a perfect hash function, collisions never arise and every search stays a single comparison.
question_patterns: In the list [34, 16, 2, 26, 80] with hash function element % 10, which two elements collide and where?
Define collision and collision resolution in hashing.
When is a hash function called perfect, and what guarantee does it give?
Name two hash function techniques other than the remainder method.
Why must the cost of computing a hash function stay small?

solution_steps.explain: Compute the hash of each element; any shared slot is a collision needing resolution, while a fully unique mapping marks the function perfect.

worked_examples.q: Two elements mapping to one hash slot is called what?

concepts.title: Sorted List Requirement for Binary Search
concepts.definition: Binary search only works when the list is already ordered, because each midpoint comparison decides which half can still hold the key; on unsorted data it would discard the wrong half, so the data must be sorted first.
concepts.formula: sorted list + mid comparison -> discard one half
concepts.key_idea: A dictionary search for Zoology starts in the second half only because the words are alphabetically arranged.
question_patterns: Why must a list be sorted before binary search can be trusted?
Activity 6.3 sorts [17, 8, -4, 7, 0, 2, 19] and searches for 7. How many iterations does binary search need?
How many key comparisons does binary search take to find -4 in the list [-4, 0, 2, 7, 8, 17, 19]?
Which real-world tools, such as dictionaries and telephone directories, behave like binary search?
Where do modified binary search techniques find use in computing systems?

solution_steps.explain: Check the list is ascending or descending; only then can each midpoint comparison safely eliminate half the candidates.

worked_examples.q: Binary search demands that the list is already what?

worked_examples.title: One-iteration hit for key 17
worked_examples.problem: In the 15-element sorted list of Example 6.2, find where binary search probes first when searching for 17, and how many iterations it needs.
worked_examples.answer_note: The probe lands on index 7 where numList[7] is 17, so the search succeeds in one iteration at position 8.

worked_examples.title: Hashing the key 16
worked_examples.problem: With a hash table of 10 slots, compute the slot of key 16 by the remainder method and the position Program 6-3 reports.
worked_examples.answer_note: Key 16 sits in slot 6 and is reported at position 7, exactly as the program output shows.
